title: Plant dashboard
summary: A telemetry dashboard for a fictional plant: 8 machines, 72 widgets, and vibration data sampled at up to 5 kHz, with spectra, percentiles, correlations and persistent alarms. The same widgets are built three ways, native, native with workers, and on Isoloop in six placements, so you can switch between them and compare. An interactive page lets you build your own widgets from a drawer.
try: Press a widget's block button. On the native builds the whole page stalls. On Isoloop's default placement all 72 widgets share a pool, so they all stall, but no data is lost and the pool restarts after 2 s. Switch to `split` and only that machine's 8 widgets stall.
Switch between Native and Isoloop in the header, and between placements, and block the same widget again.
On the Isoloop build, reload the page: the alarms and events are still there, every acknowledged record up to 10,000.
Open the interactive page and add widgets from the drawer: each one is an isolate.

On the Isoloop build, add `?devtools=1` to the address and open the devtools panel in the corner (or press Alt+Shift+D): block a widget from its Isolates view, and watch the kernel’s events and the live Messages.

blocks.heading: Desktop
findings: Isoloop moves the widgets off the main thread: it's 23–27% busy against 79–84% on the native builds, and typing answers 28–55 ms sooner.
In the default placement, `matched`, against native + workers: a 3 s block loses no data on the other machines on either build, and the page is back to normal 0.2 s sooner.
It costs CPU, memory and start-up: +11 to +19 points of CPU across threads, +40 to +51 MB after GC, and first data 0.19–0.29 s later.
blocks.caption: The plant dashboard on the desktop machine (4 cores fixed at 2.0 GHz), Chromium at 5 kHz, 5 interleaved rounds, measured at plant-v0.1.0, November 2026. Each native build is measured against the Isoloop placement shaped like it.

pairs.label: Native + workers against Isoloop matched (the default)

rows.label: Data lost on the other machines during a 3 s block
Back to normal after the block

blocks.firefox: Firefox drops 89–126 fewer late frames on Isoloop, where Chromium drops none on either build; its first data is 0.4–0.5 s later.
notes: Δ is the median of the gaps measured in each round, so it can differ from the difference of the two medians.

The native builds keep their data in a small store written for this app, with no message bus. They don't contain a blocked widget, restart a crashed one, replay data to it, check grants or schemas, or keep acknowledged history. The extra CPU and memory pay for those features.

blocks.heading: The interactive page
findings: A heavy preview in the drawer fills the native main thread (93% busy, 25 frames over 25 ms); on Isoloop it runs on the preview's own worker, the main thread is 3% busy and no frame is dropped.
The heavy preview draws 1.1 s sooner on Isoloop, and uses more CPU in total: 127% of a core against 100%.
The drawer answers slower on Isoloop: typing takes 43 ms against 7 ms on a light draft, because each keystroke goes to the drawer's worker and back.
blocks.caption: Native against Isoloop, the plant's interactive page on the desktop machine (4 cores fixed at 2.0 GHz), Chromium at 5 kHz, 5 interleaved rounds, measured at plant-v0.2.0, November 2026.
blocks.firefox: Firefox: native drops 138 frames under the heavy preview and runs at 26 fps; Isoloop drops none, and its preview draws 0.7 s sooner.

blocks.heading: Phones
findings: A flagship Android phone, in Chrome: every build holds 60 frames/s with no long tasks at both rates, so there's no responsiveness difference to report.

A mid-range Android phone (8 cores, a 96 Hz screen), in Firefox: both native builds run short, at 45–56 of a possible 96 frames/s. `matched` draws 68–77 and `one` 80–84, and typing answers in 15–23 ms against 50–64 ms at 5 kHz. Isoloop takes 1.2–2.0 s to first data, against 0.4–0.9 s.

An older iOS phone, in Safari 16.6: Isoloop doesn't run ahead of native. At 5 kHz native holds 60 frames/s (3 late), native + workers 58.5 (33 late) and `matched` 51.9 (93 late); the more workers a placement has, the further it drops.
CPU and memory weren't recorded on the phones.
blocks.caption: Recorded by hand with each page's Record 10 s panel, one round per build, at plant-v0.1.0-rc.3 and rc.5, November 2026, so these are observations rather than interleaved medians.

blocks.heading: The inspection feed
findings: What a reader on `kernel.inspect()` costs the page, as an open devtools panel or the dev MCP would be: `matched` at 5 kHz with the feed open against closed.
Leaning one way: total CPU on cross-origin isolated Chromium, where the feed also measures memory per isolate, is about +1 point at the median, the top of its spread (−7 to +1).

Memory before garbage collection is 4 MB higher with the feed open on headless Chromium (+2 to +7), higher in every round; after a forced collection the gap crosses zero on both runs. It's the one gap in the table on one side of zero.
The other figures have no gap, or spreads that cross zero. Five rounds can't separate a gap of about a point from the round-to-round spread.
Every run keeps a ring buffer of the last 200 events from the page's start, read or not: about 18 KB as JSON on Chromium and 15 KB on Firefox.

Δ is the median of the per-round gaps, with the lowest and highest round in brackets.

blocks.firefox: Firefox (no CPU or memory figures there): late frames +1 (−1 to +2) and typing +16 ms (−33 to +33), both crossing zero; recovery after the 3 s block was 110 ms faster with the feed open (−297 to −4), in all 5 rounds, which isn't explained.
notes: The feed is `@experimental`, and nothing but the ring buffer runs until something reads it. “No change” marks a gap whose spread crosses zero.
